    Where do earthquakes and volcanoes happen — and why there?¶

    EPS 88 · PyEarth. Open your own copy on DataHub: click here.

    Two files today. One holds every earthquake of magnitude 5.5 and above located from 2000 to the end of 2025; the other, every volcano the Smithsonian Institution lists as active in about the last twelve thousand years. Neither file is a map, and yet each one draws one.

    You will draw those maps from longitude and latitude, lay the plate boundaries over them, and colour every earthquake by how deep it was. Then you will turn the Andes on their side and watch a sinking plate appear. Last, you will count earthquakes by size and compare them with eruptions.

    Every place you write something opens with a pencil icon and the words Your turn, and is followed by a cell that already has the shape of the answer written in, with ... wherever your code goes. Replace every ..., run every cell so your answers and figures are saved in the file, then download this notebook itself — the .ipynb file — and upload it to Gradescope. Not a PDF: the marking reads your notebook, and a PDF cannot be read. In JupyterLab: File ▸ Download, or right-click the file in the left-hand panel and choose Download.

    Two habits from the first minute. A cell runs when you press Shift+Enter, and the notebook remembers everything it has already run — so when something breaks and you cannot see why, Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells throws the memory away and rebuilds it from the top. That is never the wrong thing to do.

    What you'll be able to do¶

    The science. Say where earthquakes and volcanoes happen and which plate boundaries they sit on, show from the side that the deep earthquakes lie on a sinking plate, and read counts that span a factor of a thousand.

    The code. Pick the rows of a table with a condition, and join several conditions with & · draw a map as plt.scatter of longitude against latitude, with layers on top · colour every dot by a column with c= and add a key with plt.colorbar · draw a side view, with depth down the page · put two panels side by side with plt.subplot, and count an axis in factors of ten with plt.yscale("log").

The cell under it has every line already started, with ... where your code goes and a comment saying what goes there.     Setup¶

    Run the next cell once; you are not expected to follow it. It reads the USGS earthquake catalogue and the Smithsonian's volcano and eruption tables from the live archives, falling back to the copy stored with the course, and three files that ship with the course: the coastlines, the plate boundaries, and a model of the sinking plate under South America.

    Every count printed in this notebook came from the copy stored with the course. The archives are revised all the time, so a slightly different number is the archive having moved, not you having made a mistake.

    1. Where do earthquakes and volcanoes happen?¶

    Longitude runs from -180 to 180 around the world and latitude from -90 to 90 up it, so a scatter plot of one against the other is already a map. plt.xlim and plt.ylim fix the edges at the whole world, and plt.gca().set_aspect("equal") draws a degree across the same length as a degree up. The coastline goes on with one plt.plot, as in the first week.

plt.plot(coast["lon"], coast["lat"], color="0.6", lw=0.6)
plt.xlim(-180, 180)
plt.ylim(-90, 90)
plt.gca().set_aspect("equal")
plt.xlabel("longitude (degrees east)")
plt.ylabel("latitude (degrees north)")

    The dots are not spread over the planet; they are lines. One rings the Pacific: Alaska, Japan, Indonesia, New Zealand, the whole west coast of the Americas. Another runs down the middle of the Atlantic, far from any coast, drawn by nothing but earthquakes.

    This map stretches the far north and south: it draws a degree of longitude the same width at every latitude, while on the ground the degrees close in towards the poles. For finding where things are, that is a fair trade.

    2. What draws those lines?¶

    The lines are the edges of the tectonic plates. plate_boundaries.csv holds those edges as longitudes and latitudes, and its kind column says how the two plates meet:

    • ridge — they pull apart, and new ocean floor forms between them;
    • transform — they slide past each other;
    • trench — one plate bends down and sinks under the other. The file also files the collision fronts of the Himalaya and the Zagros under this word, where no ocean floor sinks.

    Each kind is the rows of the table whose kind is that word. boundaries["kind"] == "ridge" asks every row the same question and hands back a mask of True and False, and boundaries[mask] keeps the rows where it is True — last week's move, on a table.

    The boundaries land on the dots: the blue ridge down the Atlantic is the line the earthquakes drew on their own, and black trenches trace most of the rim of the Pacific.

    Do the volcanoes sit on the same lines, and on which kind? The Smithsonian classifies the setting of every volcano, and the setup cell kept the first words of it in a column called setting: "Subduction zone" where a plate sinks at a trench, "Rift zone" where plates pull apart, and "Intraplate" for a volcano far from any boundary.

    69 percent of the catalogued volcanoes sit at subduction zones, and there that is a mechanism rather than a coincidence. The sinking plate carries water down, locked inside its minerals. Once the plate is roughly a hundred kilometres deep, the water is driven out into the hot mantle above it, and water lowers the temperature at which rock melts, so mantle that would have stayed solid melts. The melt rises and builds a line of volcanoes set back from the trench.

    The blue rift volcanoes (18 percent) sit where plates pull apart: on the ridge through Iceland and along the rift down East Africa, and the orange ones (12 percent) sit far from any line, like Hawaii in the middle of the Pacific. The catalogue lists volcanoes people can find and name, mostly on land, while most of the magma Earth erupts comes out along the mid-ocean ridges, under kilometres of water, where eruptions are rarely seen.

    3. Where are the deep earthquakes, and why there?¶

    Every earthquake in the catalogue also has a depth, in kilometres. Seismologists sort them into three classes: shallow, down to 70 km; intermediate, 70 to 300 km; and deep, below 300 km. Deep earthquakes are strange: a few hundred kilometres down, rock is hot and under enormous pressure, and it should not break the way rock near the surface does. So where they happen is a clue.

    785 of 12847 earthquakes are deeper than 300 km: 6 percent

    Only 6 percent of the earthquakes are deep, and they are not scattered: nearly every cluster of dark dots lies beside a black trench line, and along the ridge down the Atlantic every dot is pale. But the dark dots are not on the trench lines. They sit off to one side of them.

    A map cannot show which way that is going, so turn one stretch of trench on its side. First, pick the stretch: the earthquakes under southern Peru, Chile, Bolivia and Argentina.

    ✏️ Your turn 3¶

    Pick the earthquakes in one box.

    A box needs four conditions, one for each edge: latitude greater than -30 and less than -15, longitude greater than -80 and less than -60. Each condition is a mask; join them with &, which keeps a row only when all four are True. Put each condition in its own brackets: Python does & before > and <, so without them it would join the wrong pieces and stop with an error. The map under the cell shows the box you picked.

    Use these names, because the self-check looks for them: andes.

    The earthquakes below 70 km roughly follow the black line: under the coast the plate is some 37 km down, and it keeps sinking eastwards to more than 500 km. The deepest cluster lies a little further south, near 27°S, where Slab2 takes the plate to about 620 km. This is the Nazca plate, the floor of the eastern Pacific, going down beneath South America. A slab is a plate that has sunk into the mantle, usually at a trench; the deep earthquakes happen inside slabs. A slab stays colder than the mantle around it for millions of years, which is thought to be why it can still break at those depths; exactly how rock breaks 600 km down is still argued about.

    4. How many small ones for each big one?¶

    That was where; now how big. Volcanologists score an eruption on the Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI), a whole number from 0 up, and the eruption table carries it in ExplosivityIndexMax. An index counts steps, not amounts: from VEI 2 up, each step is about ten times the ash and pumice thrown out, and each step of magnitude about 32 times the energy. So Tambora's great eruption (VEI 7) threw out about a hundred times the ash and pumice of Mount St Helens in 1980 (VEI 5). The tenfold step is how Newhall and Self defined the VEI in 1982; the 32 comes from Gutenberg and Richter's relation between magnitude and energy.

    The cell below counts the eruptions in each class, and draws the counts twice, side by side. plt.subplot(1, 2, k) splits a figure into one row of two panels and draws in panel k. The left panel counts its axis the ordinary way; plt.yscale("log") makes the right one count in factors of ten.

The two smallest classes fall short of that line, most likely because a small eruption long ago, far from anyone, left nothing to record.

    Only 28 of 12,847 reach magnitude 8. On the log axis the earthquake bars fall in a roughly straight line too: below magnitude 8, each whole step holds about 7 to 11 times fewer earthquakes than the step below. Eruptions and earthquakes are rare in the same way: every step up the scale is several times rarer, by a roughly steady factor. Since each step multiplies the size, the count falls as a power of the size: a power law. On an ordinary axis it hides everything big; on a log axis it is a line, and in week 7 that line becomes a forecast of how often the biggest ones come.

    The question, answered¶

    Earthquakes and volcanoes happen along the edges of the tectonic plates: the earthquakes drew those lines before the boundary file did, and 69 percent of the catalogued volcanoes sit at subduction zones, where water carried down by a sinking plate lowers the melting point of the mantle above it. Turned on its side, the Andes show why the deep earthquakes sit inland of the trench: they happen inside the Nazca plate as it sinks beneath South America. And the big events are rare in a regular way — each step up in size several times rarer — which only a log axis shows.

    Week 4 summary¶

    The science¶

    Where do earthquakes and volcanoes happen — and why there?
    Earthquakes and volcanoes sit on plate boundaries; the deep earthquakes lie on slabs sinking beneath the trenches. Pick the plot for the question: a map for where, a side view for how deep, a log axis for how many. Big eruptions and big earthquakes are rare in the same way: each step up the scale is several times rarer, so their counts fall as a roughly straight line on a log axis.

    • Log axes. When the values span factors of a thousand, plot the exponents instead and a curve becomes a line.
    • Index scale. An index counts steps, not amounts: from VEI 2 up, each step is about ten times the ash and pumice thrown out, and each step of magnitude about 32 times the energy.
    • Slab. A slab is a plate that has sunk into the mantle, usually at a trench; the deep earthquakes happen inside slabs.

    The code¶

    Function What it does
    NumPy
    mask & other_mask True only where both masks are True, the array version of and
    np.histogram(values, bins) the counts a histogram would draw, handed back as numbers instead of drawn
    pandas
    table[mask] keep only the rows where the mask is True
    column.count() / column.median() how many, and the middle value
    Matplotlib
    plt.figure(figsize=(w, h)) start a new figure, w inches wide and h tall — the first line of every plot cell
    plt.subplot(rows, cols, k) draw several panels in one figure; k picks which one
    plt.bar(positions, heights) one bar per category — the right chart when the bottom axis is a label
    plt.yscale("log") count the axis in factors of ten, so classes a thousandfold apart are all readable
    plt.scatter(x, y, c=values, cmap=...) colour every dot by a third column, with vmin/vmax fixing what the ends mean
    plt.colorbar(label=...) the key that says what the colours mean
    plt.hist(values, bins) draw how the numbers are spread; bins is either how many to use, or the edges to use
    plt.axvline(x) a vertical line at x, to mark a boundary on a plot

    What the numbers mean. Under Japan the deep earthquakes sit about 5.5 degrees west of the shallow ones, where under the Andes they sat about 8 degrees east. The side view shows why the sign flips: the deep dots slope down towards the west, so the plate under Japan sinks westwards, where the Nazca plate sinks eastwards under South America. In both places the deep earthquakes lie on the side away from the ocean the plate came from. The median is a blunt tool, though: this box holds more than one stretch of trench, and a different box could move the gap.

    ✓ Homework 2 — the deepest earthquake under the Himalaya is 69 km down, against 586 km under Japan

    What the numbers mean. No. The deepest earthquake under the Himalaya is 69 km down, against 586 km under Japan, and none of the 83 is deeper than 70 km, while Japan's band runs down to nearly 600 km. That fits the Himalaya being a collision of continents: continental rock is light, and does not sink into the mantle the way ocean floor does, so there is no deep slab to break. The box leaves out the Hindu Kush and the Pamir, west of it, where the same collision does make earthquakes more than 200 km down, so this is one stretch, not every collision. What the earthquakes cannot show is how far north, and how deep, India's plate reaches beneath Tibet; seismologists image that from how seismic waves travel through the rock.

    What the numbers mean. 189 of the 231 volcanoes that have erupted since 2000, 82 percent, are at subduction zones, more than the 69 percent of the whole catalogue: the red triangles crowd the rim of the Pacific. The numbers leave open how much of that is the Earth and how much the record. An eruption on the sea floor, kilometres down, is rarely seen or dated, and the ridges, where most magma comes out, barely appear in either list. Watching the sea floor itself would settle it.
